questions.q: Meena marks two points A and B on a sheet and joins them first by a wavy path and then by a straight path drawn with a ruler. She calls the straight one 'the line segment AB'. What makes her right?
questions.a: It is the shortest path from A to B, and it includes A and B as its end points
o: It is the shortest path from A to B, and it includes A and B as its end points
It is the only path that carries on past A and past B without any end
It is the only path that can be named BA as well as AB, and the wavy one cannot
It is the only path that has a starting point and no second end point

questions.q: Milestones P, Q, R and S stand in this order along a straight road. Ravi says, 'The segment RP is a different segment from PR, because a bus on it starts at R and the other starts at P.' Which reply is correct?
questions.a: RP and PR are the same segment, with the same two end points and the same length, and Q lies on it
o: RP and PR are the same segment, with the same two end points and the same length, and Q lies on it
RP is a different segment, and it does not contain Q because it starts at R and moves away from P
RP is a ray, since it starts at R, and PR is the segment since it starts at P
RP and PR are the same segment, but Q does not lie on it because Q is not an end point

questions.q: Kabir draws a very thick dot with a marker and says, 'this point is 3 mm wide and 3 mm tall.' Which correction is right?
questions.a: A point has no length, breadth or height; the dot is only a model of a precise location
o: A point has no length, breadth or height; the dot is only a model of a precise location
A point has length but no breadth, so the dot should be drawn as a short thin line
A point is any dot wider than the tip of a sharp pencil, so Kabir is nearly right
A point is the shortest path between two marks, so one dot cannot be a point

questions.q: Points A, B and C lie along one straight edge of a ruler. Tara draws the line through A and B, Bela draws the line through B and C, and Chitra draws the line through A and C. How many different lines have the three girls drawn?
questions.a: Only one, because any two of the points fix the same line
o: Only one, because any two of the points fix the same line
Three, one for each pair of points
Two, because two girls must have repeated each other and the third is new
Six, because each line can also be read the other way round

questions.q: P and Q are two points and R is another point lying on the line PQ. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: The line through P and R is the same line as the line PQ
o: The line through P and R is the same line as the line PQ
The line through P and R is a different line that meets line PQ only at P
The line through P and R is only the part of line PQ between P and R
No line can pass through both P and R because R is already on line PQ

questions.q: Seven points are joined one after another in a chain by six line segments. The number of points that lie on exactly two of the segments is ___.

Consider these statements about points, segments and lines.
Statement 1: A line segment AB and a line AB both have exactly two end points, A and B.
Statement 2: The line segment from B to A is the same as the line segment from A to B.
Statement 3: Exactly one line passes through two given points.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 only
all three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A drawing of a line on a page can never show the whole line.
Reason (R): A line is a line segment extended in both directions without any end, but the page has edges.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Three points A, B and C lie on one line with B between A and C. (a) Name every line segment that has two of these points as its end points. (b) How many different lines pass through all three points?
questions.a: (a) AB, BC and AC. (b) Exactly one line, because two points already fix a line and the third point lies on it.
s: Part (a): the three segments AB, BC and AC
Part (b): one line, with the reason that two points fix a line

questions.q: The line segment AB measures 7 cm. Asha says, 'The line AB is longer than the segment AB, so it measures about 12 cm.' (a) Can any length be given for the line AB? (b) Which of the two figures has the length 7 cm, and what is it that Asha is really comparing?
questions.a: (a) No. The line AB has no end in either direction, so no length can be given for it, not even 12 cm. (b) The segment AB has the length 7 cm, since it stops at A and B. Asha is comparing the part of the line that she can see on the page, which is only a piece, with the segment; the whole line cannot be measured.
s: Says no length can be given for the line because it never ends
Gives 7 cm to the segment and says what she compared was a drawn piece of the line

questions.q: True or False: Two different lines can both pass through the same two points A and B. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Any two points determine a unique line that passes through both of them, so a second line through A and B would be the same line.
s: Verdict False
Reason: two points determine exactly one line

questions.q: Points K, L, M and N are joined in a chain by the segments KL, LM and MN. (a) Name the points that lie on exactly one segment and the points that lie on exactly two. (b) A point S is added and the segment NS is drawn. Which points now lie on exactly one segment?
questions.a: (a) K and N lie on exactly one segment; L and M lie on exactly two. (b) Now N lies on two segments (MN and NS), so only K and S lie on exactly one segment.
s: Part (a): K and N on one, L and M on two
Part (b): K and S now on one, because N has moved to two

questions.q: Ruchi draws a line through P and Q right across a long strip of paper from one edge to the other and says, 'I have drawn the whole line PQ.' Pooja draws a short straight stroke that stops exactly at P and at Q and says, 'This is too small to be the segment PQ.' Judge both girls.
questions.a: Ruchi is wrong: a line has no end, so what she has drawn stops at the edges of the strip and is only a piece of the line PQ. Pooja is wrong too: the segment PQ is exactly the part with P and Q as end points, so her stroke is the complete segment PQ however short it is.
s: Ruchi wrong: only a part of an endless line is drawn
Pooja wrong: a segment stops at its end points, so her stroke is complete

questions.q: Tanvi says, 'Any three points always give three different lines.' Test her claim with (i) three points on a straight edge and (ii) three points not on one line, and say whether she is right.
questions.a: Partly right. If the points are not on one line, each pair gives its own line: AB, BC and CA, that is 3 lines. If the three points are on one line, every pair gives that same line, so there is only 1 line. Her claim holds only for points not on one line.
s: Case (ii): 3 lines AB, BC, CA
Case (i): 1 line, because every pair fixes the same line
Verdict: right only when the points are not on one line

questions.q: Four villages A, B, C and D have no three in a straight line. Write a situation, using these villages, that has exactly 6 line segments in it, and explain where the 6 comes from.
questions.a: A panchayat lays a straight footpath directly between every two of the four villages. The pairs are AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD, which makes 6 segments (a path from A to B is the same as from B to A).
s: A consistent situation with the four villages
Lists the 6 pairs or counts 4 x 3 / 2
Says AB and BA are counted once

questions.q: Rahul draws a thick pencil line and a thin ink line through the same two points A and B, so close together that they cannot be told apart, and says, 'These are the same line, because only one line passes through two given points.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Yes. Two points fix exactly one line, so every line through A and B is that same line. The thick and the thin strokes are two drawings of it that differ only in width, and a line has no width.
s: Uses: two points fix exactly one line
Explains the two strokes as drawings of one line
Verdict Yes with the reason that a line has no width

questions.q: Four points A, C, B and D lie in this order along one straight line with AC = 3 cm, CB = 5 cm and BD = 2 cm. (a) What is the length of the segment AB, and of the segment AD? (b) Write every line segment that has two of these four points as end points and give its length. (c) Sunil says 'the line segment CD is 7 cm and it contains the point B.' Is he right? (d) Name the line that passes through A and D and say whether it is the same as the line through C and B. (e) Show that no two of the segments in (b) have the same length.
questions.a: (a) AB = 3 + 5 = 8 cm and AD = 8 + 2 = 10 cm. (b) AC 3, CB 5, AB 8, BD 2, CD 5 + 2 = 7, AD 10: six segments. (c) Yes: CD = CB + BD = 5 + 2 = 7 cm and B lies between C and D. (d) The line AD; it is the same as the line CB because the two points C and B lie on it and two points fix one line. (e) The six lengths 3, 5, 8, 2, 7, 10 are all different.
s: Part (a): AB = 8 cm and AD = 10 cm
Part (b): six segments with lengths 3, 5, 8, 2, 7, 10
Part (c): CD = 7 cm and B lies on it
Part (d): same line, since two points fix one line
Part (e): the six lengths are all different

questions.q: Rihan marks one point and Sheetal marks two points on a sheet. (a) How many lines can Rihan draw through his point? (b) How many can Sheetal draw through both of hers? (c) Three points are marked not on one line: how many lines can be drawn through pairs of them? (d) Three points are marked on one line: how many? (e) Explain, using what you found in (b), why the answers to (c) and (d) differ.
questions.a: (a) As many as he likes (more than can be counted). (b) Exactly one. (c) 3 lines. (d) 1 line. (e) Two points fix a unique line. In (c) the three pairs lie on three different lines; in (d) every pair lies on the one line that already holds all three points.
s: Part (a): many lines
Part (b): exactly one line
Part (c): 3 lines
Part (d): 1 line
Part (e): links the difference to two points fixing a unique line

questions.q:
Five poles A, B, C, D and E stand in this order along a straight road, with AB = 40 m, BC = 60 m, CD = 50 m and DE = 30 m. A cable fault has to be found by checking a line segment of the cable. Each separate check costs Rs 400 to set up, plus Rs 15 for every metre checked.
(a) Find the length of the segment AE and of the segment BD.
(b) A first report says the fault lies between B and D. Find the cost of checking BD in one go, and the cost of checking BC and CD as two separate checks.
(c) A second report says the fault lies between C and E. If both reports are true, which segment must contain the fault, and how long is it?
(d) Find the cost of checking that segment alone. Should the crew trust both reports and check only that segment, or check BD? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) AE = 40 + 60 + 50 + 30 = 180 m and BD = 60 + 50 = 110 m. (b) BD in one go: 400 + 110 x 15 = Rs 2,050. Two separate checks: 2 x 400 + 110 x 15 = Rs 2,450, which is Rs 400 more. (c) The fault is on both the segment BD and the segment CE, so it is on the part they share, the segment CD of 50 m. (d) Checking CD alone costs 400 + 50 x 15 = Rs 1,150, which is Rs 900 less than checking BD. Checking CD is cheaper, but if either report may be wrong, the fault could be outside CD and a second check would be needed. Either choice is accepted with a stated reason.
s: Part (a): 180 m and 110 m
Part (b): Rs 2,050 against Rs 2,450
Part (c): the shared segment CD of 50 m
Part (d): Rs 1,150 and a reasoned choice about trusting the reports

questions.q:
A surveyor drives 5 pegs P, Q, R, S and T into a field. The pegs P, Q, R and S stand in that order along one straight boundary and T lies off it. She wants every pair of pegs joined, and she has 7 strings.
(a) How many different line segments have two of the pegs as end points?
(b) How many different lines pass through at least two of the pegs?
(c) Why is the count in (b) smaller than the count in (a)?
(d) She can either cut one string for each segment, or stretch one string along each line, running past the end pegs. Which plan can she carry out with 7 strings, and does it still join every pair of pegs?
questions.a: (a) 10 segments (PQ, PR, PS, QR, QS, RS, TP, TQ, TR, TS). (b) 5 lines: one line holds P, Q, R and S, and T gives 4 more lines. (c) The six segments among P, Q, R and S all lie on one line, so they give 1 line instead of 6. (d) The segment plan needs 10 strings, which she does not have. The line plan needs 5 strings, so it is possible with 2 spare, and every pair of pegs lies on a stretched string, so every pair is joined.
s: Part (a): 10 segments
Part (b): 5 lines
Part (c): six segments share one line
Part (d): 10 strings against 5 strings, so the line plan

questions.q: A torch at point T shines along a straight path that passes through a lamp-post P and then, further on, a tree Q. Which name describes the same beam as ray TP?
questions.a: Ray TQ, because both start at T and go the same way
o: Ray TQ, because both start at T and go the same way
Ray QT, because it uses the same two letters Q and T
Ray PT, because T and P are both on the beam
Ray PQ, because P and Q are both on the beam

questions.q: Neha names the angle whose arms are the rays KP and KR as ∠PRK. A classmate says this is wrong. What is the mistake?
questions.a: The vertex K must be the middle letter, so the name should be ∠PKR or ∠RKP
o: The vertex K must be the middle letter, so the name should be ∠PKR or ∠RKP
The letters must be in alphabetical order, so it should be ∠KPR, with the vertex named first
P and R lie on the same arm, so the name needs another point on the second arm
An angle can only be named by one letter, so it should be ∠K, the letter of the vertex

questions.q: Points A, B, C and D lie in this order on one straight line. Which statement about rays on this line is correct?
questions.a: Rays AB, AC and AD are one and the same ray, but ray DA is a different ray
o: Rays AB, AC and AD are one and the same ray, but ray DA is a different ray
Ray AB and ray BA are the same ray, because both lie on this one line and use the same two letters
Ray BC and ray CD are the same ray, because C and D both lie beyond B on the line
Ray AD and ray DA are the same ray, because a ray can be named from either of its two letters

questions.q: On a page, three rays PA, PB and PC start from the same point P. Why can the angle between rays PA and PB not simply be called ∠P?
questions.a: P is the vertex of several angles here, so ∠P would not say which one
o: P is the vertex of several angles here, so ∠P would not say which one
The vertex of an angle can never be used on its own, even when only one angle is formed there
∠P is the name of the angle formed by rays PB and PC alone, as the middle ray gives the name
A name must always carry a point from each arm, so a single letter is never allowed

questions.q: Ray OA starts at O, and a point B lies on this ray. Raju writes: 'This ray can be called ray OB.' Meera writes: 'This ray can be called ray AO.' Who is right?
questions.a: Raju only, since B lies on the ray from O, so ray OB is the same ray
o: Raju only, since B lies on the ray from O, so ray OB is the same ray
Meera only, since ray AO uses the same two letters as ray OA does
Both, since a ray can be named from either end by its two letters
Neither, since a ray has to be named with all three points O, A and B together

questions.q: Points P, Q, R, S and T lie in this order along a line. The number of these five points that lie on the ray starting at Q and passing through R is ___.

Read these statements about rays and angles.
Statement 1: If B lies on ray OA, then ray OB is the same ray as ray OA.
Statement 2: Ray OA and ray AO are the same ray because they use the same two letters.
Statement 3: ∠EBD and ∠DBE name the same angle, whose vertex is B.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
all three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An angle is formed by two rays that start from different points.
Reason (R): In the name ∠DBE, the vertex B is written as the middle letter.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q:
Match each description in Column I with its name in Column II. M, N and K are three points that are not on one line.
Column I: 1. The ray starting at M and passing through N  2. The ray starting at N and passing through M  3. The angle with vertex N whose arms pass through M and K  4. The shortest path from M to N including both
Column II: A. line segment MN  B. ray NM  C. ray MN  D. ∠MNK
(a) Name the ray that starts at C and passes through D. (b) Can the ray that starts at D and passes through C be given the same name? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Ray CD. (b) No. It starts at D, not at C, so it is a different ray, written DC with the starting point first.
s: Part (a): ray CD, starting point first
Part (b): No, because the starting point is different

questions.q: True or False: The angle with vertex M and arms through points N and K can be named ∠NMK or ∠KMN, but it cannot be named ∠MNK. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The vertex is always the middle letter. ∠MNK would have N as its vertex, which is a different angle.
s: Verdict True
Reason: the vertex must be the middle letter, and ∠MNK has vertex N

questions.q: Mohan draws an angle whose vertex is Y and whose arms pass through X and Z, and writes it in his notebook as ∠YXZ. (a) Which point does that name make the vertex? (b) Write the angle correctly in two ways, and say why ∠YXZ cannot be the same angle.
questions.a: (a) The middle letter is the vertex, so ∠YXZ has its vertex at X. (b) ∠XYZ or ∠ZYX. ∠YXZ is formed by the rays XY and XZ, which start at X, so it is a different angle from the one with vertex Y.
s: Middle letter X is the vertex in his name
Gives ∠XYZ and ∠ZYX and notes the vertex differs so the angle differs

questions.q: Gita says, 'A torch beam is a line segment, because the light stops where it hits the wall.' Ruchi says it is better modelled by a ray. Who is nearer the truth, and what does the wall change and what does it not change?
questions.a: Ruchi is nearer: the beam starts at the torch and goes on in one direction, which is a ray. The wall only stops us seeing the light; it does not give the beam a second end point, which a line segment must have.
s: Chooses ray: one starting point and goes on in one direction
The wall hides the light but is not an end point of the beam, unlike a segment's end points

questions.q: A pair of scissors is opened to cut cloth. (a) Which part of the scissors is the vertex of the angle? (b) Which parts are its arms, and what happens to the size of the angle as the blades open wider?
questions.a: (a) The point where the two blades are joined. (b) The two blades are the arms. As the blades are turned further apart the amount of turn increases, so the angle becomes larger.
s: Part (a): the joint of the blades is the vertex
Part (b): blades as arms, and more turning means a larger angle

questions.q: Imran says, 'Ray PQ and ray QP are the same ray because they use the same two points.' Take R on the line beyond Q (so that P, Q, R lie in that order) and test his claim.
questions.a: No. Ray PQ starts at P and passes through Q and on past R, so R lies on it. Ray QP starts at Q and goes the other way through P, so R does not lie on it. The two rays start at different points, so they are different rays.
s: Ray PQ contains R
Ray QP does not contain R
Verdict No: different starting points

questions.q: The points P, Q and R lie in this order on a straight line and S is a point off the line. Aman says, 'Ray PQ and ray RS form an angle because they are close to each other.' (a) Show that they do not form an angle. (b) Name an angle that has ray RS as one arm and a ray along the line as the other, and say why ∠SRQ and ∠SRP are the same angle.
questions.a: (a) An angle needs two rays with a common starting point. Ray PQ starts at P and ray RS starts at R, which is a different point, so there is no vertex and no angle. (b) ∠SRQ (or ∠SRP). Q lies between P and R, so ray RQ goes towards P and passes through it; ray RQ and ray RP are the same ray, so ∠SRQ and ∠SRP have the same arms and are the same angle.
s: Common starting point needed; P and R differ, so no angle
Names ∠SRQ or ∠SRP with vertex R
Ray RQ and ray RP are the same ray since Q is between P and R

questions.q: Describe an everyday object, not a pair of scissors, in which an angle is formed by turning, and name its vertex and its two arms.
questions.a: A laptop being opened: the hinge is the vertex, the keyboard base is one arm and the screen is the other arm. The more the screen is turned, the larger the angle. (Any consistent object, such as a door, is accepted.)
s: A valid object
Vertex correctly placed at the point of joining
Both arms identified

questions.q: Point M lies on ray OA between O and A, and point N lies on ray OB between O and B. (a) Write four different names for the angle formed by the rays OA and OB, using the points M, A, N and B. (b) Tara moves M beyond A on the same ray and says the angle has changed. Is she right? (c) Siya says ∠MAN is another name for this angle. Is she right? (d) Why can ∠BOA and ∠AOB be counted as one angle? (e) Why can the angle at O never be written ∠OMB?
questions.a: (a) ∠AOB, ∠MOB, ∠AON, ∠MON (and the same with the letters reversed, such as ∠BOA). (b) No: M is still on ray OA, so the arms of the angle are the same rays and the angle is the same. (c) No: in ∠MAN the vertex is A, the middle letter, so it is a different angle with arms AM and AN. (d) Both have vertex O and the same two arms. (e) In a name the vertex is the middle letter, so ∠OMB has its vertex at M, not at O.
s: Part (a): ∠AOB, ∠MOB, ∠AON, ∠MON
Part (b): not changed, same rays
Part (c): not the same, vertex A
Part (d): same vertex and same arms
Part (e): middle letter is the vertex

questions.q: Three rays OA, OB and OC start from the point O. (a) Name the three angles formed by taking the rays two at a time. (b) Is the ray AO the same as ray OA? Why? (c) A point D lies on ray OB beyond B. Is ray OD the same as ray OB? (d) A student names ∠AOB as ∠O. Say when this would be acceptable and when it would not. (e) What would you change in the picture to make '∠O' unambiguous?
questions.a: (a) ∠AOB, ∠BOC and ∠AOC. (b) No: ray AO starts at A, ray OA starts at O. (c) Yes: D lies on the ray, so it has the same starting point and goes the same way. (d) It is clear only when O is the vertex of just one angle in the picture; here O is the vertex of three. (e) Keep only two rays at O.
s: Part (a): the three angles
Part (b): No, different starting points
Part (c): Yes, same start and direction
Part (d): ambiguous when more than one angle at O
Part (e): only two rays from O

questions.q:
A park has a fountain at F. Straight paths run from F to the gate A, the library B and the canteen C, and a plate is to be fixed for every angle between two paths. The plate for ∠AFB also serves for ∠BFA, and each plate costs Rs 15. The committee has Rs 100.
(a) How many plates are needed for the three paths?
(b) What do they cost?
(c) A fourth path, to the pond D, is added. How many plates are needed now, and what do they cost?
(d) A fifth path to the playground E is planned, with the paths A, B, C, D, E leaving F in that order all round F. Compare plating every angle with plating only the angles between neighbouring paths, and recommend one.
questions.a: (a) 3 plates: ∠AFB, ∠BFC, ∠AFC. (b) 3 x 15 = Rs 45. (c) 6 angles (∠AFB, ∠AFC, ∠AFD, ∠BFC, ∠BFD, ∠CFD), so Rs 90, within Rs 100. (d) Every angle among 5 paths is 10 angles, Rs 150, which is Rs 50 over. Neighbouring paths give 5 angles (∠AFB, ∠BFC, ∠CFD, ∠DFE, ∠EFA), Rs 75, within Rs 100. Recommend the 5 neighbour plates: the other angles can be read by joining neighbouring ones. Any reasoned plan within the facts is accepted.
s: Part (a): 3 plates
Part (b): Rs 45
Part (c): 6 plates and Rs 90, within Rs 100
Part (d): Rs 150 against Rs 75 and a reasoned choice

questions.q:
A harbour has a jetty C, a signal post S, and two ships A and B, all on one straight line in the order C, S, A, B. The distances are CS 4 km, SA 5 km and AB 3 km. A searchlight sends a beam as a ray from where it stands and its light is usable up to 10 km.
(a) Which of the points A, B and C lie on ray SA?
(b) How far from S is the ship B along ray SA?
(c) A buoy D lies off the line. The beam at S turns from ray SA to ray SD. Name the angle and its vertex and arms.
(d) The master wants both ships lit and also the jetty. Each lamp costs Rs 40,000 and his budget is Rs 90,000. Compare plan X, one lamp at C aimed at A; plan Y, two lamps at S, one aimed at A and one at C; and plan Z, plan Y with a third lamp at C aimed at A as a spare. Which should he choose?
questions.a: (a) A and B lie on ray SA; C does not (it is behind S). (b) 5 + 3 = 8 km. (c) ∠ASD (or ∠DSA), vertex S, arms SA and SD. (d) Plan X costs Rs 40,000, but it lights S and A (4 and 9 km) while B is 12 km away, beyond the 10 km range, so a ship is missed. Plan Y costs Rs 80,000 and lights A and B (5 and 8 km) and C (4 km), so all three are covered within the budget. Plan Z costs Rs 1,20,000, over the budget. He should choose plan Y.
s: Part (a): A and B, not C
Part (b): 8 km
Part (c): ∠ASD with vertex S and arms SA, SD
Part (d): X misses B (12 km), Z is over Rs 90,000, Y covers all for Rs 80,000

questions.q:
Read these statements about comparing angles.
Statement 1: If two angles are placed with their vertices together and one pair of arms along each other, and the other arms also fall on each other, the angles are equal.
Statement 2: Drawing longer arms on an angle makes the angle larger.
Statement 3: Two angles that look almost the same can always be compared correctly by eye alone.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
2 only

questions.q: Ira draws ∠PQR with arms 5 cm long and Jay draws ∠XYZ with arms 9 cm long. Jay places Y on Q and ray YX along ray QP, and finds that ray YZ falls exactly along ray QR. What is true?
questions.a: Equal, as the arms fall on each other whatever their lengths
o: Equal, as the arms fall on each other whatever their lengths
Jay's angle is larger, because its arms are longer than Ira's arms
Ira's angle is larger, because its arms are shorter and so closer together
Nothing can be said until the arms are cut to the same length as one another

questions.q: A slit in the shape of an angle is cut in a card and the slit is longer than any of the straws below. Which rotating arm passes through it?
questions.a: The arm whose angle equals the slit's, even if its straws are short
o: The arm whose angle equals the slit's, even if its straws are short
The arm with the longest straws, because it fills the slit best of all
The arm whose angle is a little smaller than the slit's angle, as it is thinner
The arm whose angle is a little larger than the slit's angle, as it is wider

questions.q: A transparent circle is placed with its centre on the vertex O of angle 1, whose arms cut the edge at A and B (B is on the left of OA). The circle is then placed with its centre on the vertex of angle 2 so that one arm of angle 2 passes through A. The other arm of angle 2 cuts the edge at a point on the left of OA, beyond B. What follows?
questions.a: Angle 2 is larger, as its second arm has turned further from OA
o: Angle 2 is larger, as its second arm has turned further from OA
Angle 2 is smaller than angle 1, because its arm cuts the circle further away from A

Nothing follows until the arms of angle 2 are made as long as those of angle 1

questions.q: Pooja redraws her angle with arms 10 cm long instead of 4 cm and says, 'now my angle is bigger.' What is the correct response?
questions.a: Unchanged, as the turn from one arm to the other is the same
o: Unchanged, as the turn from one arm to the other is the same
The angle is bigger, because the longer arms cover more of the page
The angle is smaller, because longer arms lie closer together
The angle cannot be compared with the old one because the arms differ

questions.q: Four students explain how they compared two paper angles by superimposition. Exactly one explanation contains a faulty step. Which one is faulty?
questions.a: Tina: 'The second angle has the longer arms, so I put it down as the larger angle.'
o: Tina: 'The second angle has the longer arms, so I put it down as the larger angle.'
Uma: 'I put the vertices on each other and one arm of each on the other, then saw which second arm fell outside.'
Vik: 'After matching the vertex and one arm, the angle whose other arm lay inside was the smaller one.'
Wasim: 'When the second arms fell exactly on each other, I wrote that the angles are equal.'

questions.q: The straws of a rotating arm are shortened from 8 cm to 5 cm without moving the paper clip. The angle of the arm changes by ___ degrees.

Assertion (A): A transparent circle with its centre on the vertex can be used to compare two angles without superimposing them.
Reason (R): The size of an angle depends on the lengths of its arms.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Two angles look almost the same size. (a) Why is eye comparison unreliable here? (b) Name one method of the chapter that settles it.
questions.a: (a) When the amounts of turn are very close, the eye cannot tell whether one arm is a little outside the other, so the difference is not visible. (b) Superimposition, or the transparent circle method.
s: Part (a): the difference is too small to see
Part (b): superimposition or the transparent circle

questions.q: True or False: ∠PQR is placed on ∠ABC with Q on B and ray QP along ray BA, and ray QR falls inside ∠ABC. Ria says ∠PQR is larger than ∠ABC because it is packed inside it. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The angle whose second arm falls inside the other angle needs less turn from the common arm, so ∠PQR is smaller than ∠ABC. Being inside it does not make it larger.
s: Verdict False
Correction: the arm that falls inside needs less turn, so the angle is smaller

questions.q: Rays OA, OX, OY and OB come out from O in this order, one after the other. (a) Compare ∠XOY with ∠AOB and give a reason. (b) Compare ∠AOB with ∠XOB.
questions.a: (a) ∠AOB is larger, because it takes in ∠XOY along with ∠AOX and ∠YOB. (b) ∠AOB is larger, because it takes in ∠XOB along with ∠AOX.
s: Part (a): ∠AOB larger, since ∠XOY lies inside it
Part (b): ∠AOB larger, since ∠XOB lies inside it

questions.q: A slit is 10 cm long, and an arm passes through it only if its angle equals the slit's angle and its straws are shorter than the slit. Arm A has 6 cm straws and an angle larger than the slit's; arm B has 12 cm straws and an angle equal to the slit's; arm C has 9 cm straws and an angle equal to the slit's. (a) Which arm passes as it is? (b) For each of the other two, say what would fix it, or why nothing can.
questions.a: (a) Arm C only. (b) Arm B has the right angle but its straws are too long, so trimming them to under 10 cm fixes it without changing the angle. Arm A has short straws but its angle is larger than the slit's; trimming or lengthening straws does not change an angle, so it must be rebuilt with a smaller angle.
s: Arm C only
B fixed by trimming; A cannot be fixed by length and needs a new angle

questions.q: Hari does not believe that shortening the straws of a rotating arm leaves the angle unchanged. Describe how he can check this, and what he will find.
questions.a: He can trim the straws without moving the clip, and superimpose the trimmed arm on its old position or try it in the same slit. The vertex and both arms fall on the same rays, so the angle is the same and it still fits the slit.
s: Trims the straws without turning the arms
Checks by superimposing or fitting the slit, and finds the angle unchanged

questions.q: Dev says, 'The angle drawn with 10 cm arms is larger than the angle drawn with 6 cm arms.' Say whether his claim is justified and how he should compare them.
questions.a: No. The size of an angle is the amount of turn about the vertex, not the lengths of the arms, so the longer arms do not make a larger angle. He should superimpose them with the vertices together and one pair of arms matching and see which other arm falls outside.
s: Verdict No: arm length does not decide the size
Size is the amount of turn
Proposes superimposition as the check

questions.q: Show that a rotating arm whose angle is larger than the slit's angle cannot pass through the slit, however short its straws are.
questions.a: When the arm is lowered into the slit the vertex goes to the slit's vertex and the straws fall along the slit's sides. If the arm's angle is larger, one of its straws is turned further out than the slit's side, so it lies outside the slit and is stopped by the card. Only equal angles fall exactly in the slit.
s: Places the vertex at the slit's vertex
Shows a straw falls outside the slit's side
Concludes that only an equal angle passes, whatever the lengths

questions.q: Kiran compares two angles with a transparent circle. For the first angle the arms cut the edge of the circle at A and B. For the second angle he puts the centre on its vertex with one arm through A, and the other arm cuts the edge at a point C that lies between A and B. Kiran says, 'C is close to A, so the second angle is larger.' (a) Which angle is larger? (b) What is Kiran's error? (c) Where would C lie if the second angle were larger, and where if the two were equal?
questions.a: (a) The first angle is larger. (b) The nearer the second cut is to A, the less the arm has turned, so a cut at C between A and B means a smaller angle; Kiran has reversed the rule. (c) Larger: C beyond B, farther from A than B is. Equal: C exactly at B.
s: First angle larger
Error: a nearer cut means a smaller turn
Beyond B for larger, at B for equal

questions.q: Kavya compares six paper angles by superimposition and records: angle P fits inside angle Q; angle S matches angle Q exactly; angle Q fits inside angle R; angle R fits inside angle T; angle U fits inside angle P. (a) Which angles are equal? (b) Arrange all six from smallest to largest. (c) Which angles pass through a slit cut in the shape of angle S? (d) Without placing U on T, say how U and T compare and why. (e) Kavya never placed U directly on Q. What can she say about U and Q, and why?
questions.a: (a) Q and S. (b) U, P, then Q and S together, then R, then T. (c) Only angle Q (and S itself), since only equal angles pass. (d) U is smaller than T, because U is inside P, P inside Q, Q inside R, R inside T. (e) U is smaller than Q, because U is inside P and P is inside Q.
s: Part (a): Q and S equal
Part (b): order U, P, Q = S, R, T
Part (c): only the equal angle Q (and S)
Part (d): U smaller than T, by the chain of 'inside'
Part (e): U smaller than Q, by the chain U inside P inside Q

questions.q: Aman cuts an angle-shaped slit 10 cm long. An arm whose straws are not shorter than the slit does not fit as it is. Four rotating arms are tried: R1 has the same angle as the slit and straws of 6 cm; R2 has a slightly smaller angle and straws of 6 cm; R3 has a larger angle and straws of 3 cm; R4 has the same angle and straws of 15 cm. (a) Does R1 pass? (b) Does R2 pass? (c) Does R3 pass? (d) Why does R4 not pass as it is, and what could Aman do to it? (e) State the rule for passing in one sentence.
questions.a: (a) Yes, equal angle and shorter straws. (b) No, its angle is smaller than the slit's. (c) No, its angle is larger. (d) R4's angle is right but its straws are not shorter than the slit; shortening the straws leaves the angle unchanged, so trimmed it would pass. (e) An arm passes only if its angle equals the slit's angle and its straws are shorter than the slit.
s: Part (a): yes
Part (b): no, smaller angle
Part (c): no, larger angle
Part (d): straws too long; trimming keeps the angle
Part (e): equal angle and straws shorter than the slit

questions.q:
In a school craft week, a class must compare the angles in 3 pairs on Monday and in 12 pairs on Tuesday. Method T: trace one angle on tracing paper and superimpose it, 4 minutes per pair. Method C: use a transparent circle, which takes 10 minutes to make once, on Monday, and can be reused, and then 1 minute per pair.
(a) The circle is already made. Find the time for Tuesday's 12 pairs by each method.
(b) Find the time for Monday's 3 pairs by each method, including the making of the circle, and the least number of pairs for which Method C is then faster than T.
(c) Monday's pairs are: a right angle against an obtuse angle; two angles that look almost equal; an acute angle against a straight angle. Which pairs can be settled by eye and which need a method? Why?
(d) Only the pairs that cannot be settled by eye need a method, and on Tuesday all 12 do. Compare: tracing on Monday and the circle (made on Tuesday) on Tuesday, against making the circle on Monday and using it on both days. Which is quicker, and by how much?
questions.a: (a) T: 12 x 4 = 48 minutes; C: 12 x 1 = 12 minutes. (b) T: 3 x 4 = 12 minutes; C: 10 + 3 = 13 minutes. C is faster from 4 pairs (14 minutes against 16; for 3 pairs C is slower). (c) The first and third pairs can be settled by eye, because a right angle is smaller than an obtuse angle and an acute angle is smaller than a straight angle (the kinds differ). The pair that looks almost equal needs superimposition or the circle. (d) Tracing on Monday for the 1 pair needs 4 minutes, and the circle on Tuesday needs 10 + 12 = 22 minutes: 26 minutes in all. Making the circle on Monday needs 10 + 1 = 11 minutes on Monday and 12 on Tuesday: 23 minutes in all. So making the circle on Monday is quicker by 3 minutes, although Monday alone favours tracing.
s: Part (a): 48 and 12 minutes
Part (b): 12 and 13 minutes, and 4 pairs
Part (c): kinds differ for pairs 1 and 3; pair 2 needs a method
Part (d): 26 against 23 minutes, so the circle from Monday, by 3 minutes

questions.q:
A school makes eight rotating arms to test against a slit that is 10 cm long. An arm whose straws are not shorter than the slit does not fit as it is, but trimming the straws does not change its angle. Each arm is listed with the length of its straws and how its angle compares with the slit's angle: arm 1: 12 cm, equal; arm 2: 5 cm, equal; arm 3: 9 cm, larger; arm 4: 6 cm, smaller; arm 5: 4 cm, equal; arm 6: 15 cm, equal; arm 7: 7 cm, smaller; arm 8: 8 cm, equal.
(a) Which arms pass through the slit as they are?
(b) How many arms fail because their angle is different from the slit's?
(c) Why can trimming fix arms 1 and 6 but not arm 3, although arm 3's straws are short?
(d) The class needs at least 6 passing arms. Trimming costs Rs 4 for every centimetre cut off (a trimmed arm is cut to 9 cm), and rebuilding an arm costs Rs 20. What is the cheapest plan and what does it cost?
questions.a: (a) Arms 2, 5 and 8 (equal angle and straws shorter than 10 cm). (b) 3 arms: 3, 4 and 7. (c) Arms 1 and 6 have the right angle and only their straws are too long; shortening the straws leaves the angle unchanged, so they will fit. Arm 3 fails by its angle, and trimming cannot change an angle. (d) Trimming arm 1 from 12 cm to 9 cm costs 3 x 4 = Rs 12; trimming arm 6 from 15 cm to 9 cm costs 6 x 4 = Rs 24, more than rebuilding it for Rs 20. Three more passing arms are needed. Cheapest: trim arm 1 (Rs 12), rebuild arm 6 (Rs 20) and rebuild one of arms 3, 4 or 7 (Rs 20): Rs 52 in all. Trimming arm 6 as well would make Rs 56.
s: Part (a): arms 2, 5 and 8
Part (b): 3 arms
Part (c): trimming leaves the angle unchanged, so it cannot fix arm 3
Part (d): trim arm 1 (Rs 12), rebuild arm 6 and one other (Rs 20 each), Rs 52

questions.q:
A designer is planning a small decorative windmill with equally spaced blades, and every blade costs Rs 150 to make. She has Rs 1,300. She needs (i) at least one pair of blades at right angles to each other, (ii) at least one pair of blades forming a straight angle, and (iii) the angle between neighbouring blades to be acute.
(a) For a windmill with 8 blades, what fraction of a full turn lies between two neighbouring blades, and what type of angle is that?
(b) With 8 blades, which blade is at right angles to blade 1, and which forms a straight angle with it?
(c) Show that 4 blades fail one need and 6 blades fail another.
(d) Taking cost into account as well, which of 4, 6, 8 and 12 blades do you recommend?
questions.a: (a) 1/8 of a full turn, an acute angle. (b) Blade 3 (2/8 = 1/4 turn) is at right angles; blade 5 (4/8 = 1/2 turn) forms a straight angle. (c) With 4 blades, neighbours are 1/4 turn apart, a right angle, so need (iii) fails. With 6 blades the angles from blade 1 are 1/6, 1/3, 1/2, so blade 4 makes a straight angle but no pair makes a quarter turn, and need (i) fails. (d) 4 blades cost Rs 600 and 6 blades Rs 900, both failing a need; 8 blades cost Rs 1,200 and meet all three; 12 blades also meet all three (neighbours 1/12, three apart 1/4, six apart 1/2) but cost Rs 1,800, which is Rs 500 over. Recommend 8 blades, leaving Rs 100.
s: Part (a): 1/8 of a turn, acute
Part (b): blade 3 right angle, blade 5 straight angle
Part (c): 4 blades fail (iii), 6 blades fail (i)
Part (d): costs Rs 600, 900, 1,200, 1,800 and the choice of 8 blades

questions.q: Anil folds a paper strip with a straight edge so that the left half of the edge lies exactly on the right half, and presses a crease through the point O where the fold meets the edge. What does he find at O?
questions.a: Two equal angles, each a right angle, with the crease perpendicular to the edge
o: Two equal angles, each a right angle, with the crease perpendicular to the edge
Two equal angles, each acute, because the crease cuts the straight angle
Two unequal angles, one acute and one obtuse, because the crease is slanting
Two equal angles, each a straight angle

questions.q: A hinged flap swings from its closed position through 1/4 of a full turn, and then a gust pushes it through a further 1/8 of a full turn in the same direction. What kind of angle does the flap now make with its closed position?
questions.a: Obtuse, since 1/4 + 1/8 = 3/8 of a turn is more than a quarter and less than a half turn
o: Obtuse, since 1/4 + 1/8 = 3/8 of a turn is more than a quarter and less than a half turn
Acute, since the gust adds only a small turn of 1/8
Right, since the flap has already passed through a right angle
Straight, since 1/4 and 1/8 together reach a half turn

questions.q: Rina folds a straight angle to get a right angle, then folds the right angle in half again. Each new angle is compared with a right angle. Which statement about the two angles made by the second fold is correct?
questions.a: They are acute, each one-eighth of a full turn
o: They are acute, each one-eighth of a full turn
They are right angles, since folding never changes the kind of angle
They are right angles again, since the first fold already made a right angle
They are straight angles, since a crease is straight

questions.q: Which of these turns does NOT form an acute angle?
questions.a: One-third of a full turn
o: One-third of a full turn
One-eighth of a full turn
One-sixth of a full turn
One-tenth of a full turn

questions.q: A slanting crease is made on a sheet. Sana makes a second crease by folding the sheet so that the first crease falls exactly on itself. How many right angles are formed where the two creases cross?
questions.a: Four, because the two halves of a straight angle on each side of the first crease are equal
o: Four, because the two halves of a straight angle on each side of the first crease are equal
Two, because only one side of the first crease is folded
Three, because one angle stays acute where the creases cross
None, because the first crease was slanting

questions.q: A pointer turns through a right angle, then a straight angle, then another right angle, then another straight angle. It has made ___ half turns.

Consider these statements about angles in this chapter.
Statement 1: Folding a straight angle so that one arm lies on the other produces two acute angles.
Statement 2: An angle greater than a right angle but less than a straight angle is obtuse.
Statement 3: Two lines that meet at an acute angle are called perpendicular lines.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
all three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When a straight angle is folded so that one arm falls on the other, the crease divides it into two right angles.
Reason (R): The two angles on either side of the crease fall exactly on each other, so they are equal, and a straight angle is made of two right angles.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each turn in Column I with the kind of angle it makes in Column II.
Column I: 1. exactly a quarter turn  2. exactly a half turn  3. three-eighths of a full turn  4. one-tenth of a full turn
Column II: A. acute angle  B. straight angle  C. obtuse angle  D. right angle

Vidya opens her book cover through 1/4 of a full turn and then through a further 1/8 of a full turn. (a) Through what fraction of a full turn has the cover opened in all, and what kind of angle is that? (b) Her friend says, 'To open it to a straight angle she needs twice her first opening.' Is he right?
questions.a: (a) 1/4 + 1/8 = 3/8 of a full turn; it is more than a quarter turn (a right angle) and less than a half turn (a straight angle), so it is obtuse. (b) Yes: a straight angle is a half turn, and 1/2 = 2 x 1/4.
s: Part (a): 3/8 of a turn, obtuse
Part (b): yes, 1/2 is twice 1/4

questions.q: True or False: Every angle that is greater than a right angle is an obtuse angle. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. An obtuse angle must also be less than a straight angle. A straight angle itself (and anything larger) is greater than a right angle but is not obtuse.
s: Verdict False
Reason: obtuse also needs 'less than a straight angle'

questions.q: Anu says, 'An angle of 3/8 of a full turn is acute, because it is less than a half turn.' Test her statement by writing 3/8 as a number of eighths and comparing it with a quarter turn and a half turn.
questions.a: Her statement is wrong. A quarter turn is 2/8 and a half turn is 4/8. 3/8 lies between 2/8 and 4/8, so it is more than a right angle and less than a straight angle, which makes it obtuse. Being less than a half turn is not the test for acute; the test is being less than a quarter turn.
s: Writes quarter = 2/8 and half = 4/8 and places 3/8 between them
Concludes obtuse and states the test for acute (less than a quarter turn)

questions.q: A pointer on a dial turns by 1/8 of a full turn at every step, always in the same direction from its starting position. (a) State the kind of angle it makes with the starting position after steps 1, 2, 3 and 4. (b) After how many steps has it made a full turn?
questions.a: (a) Step 1: 1/8 turn, acute. Step 2: 2/8 = 1/4 turn, a right angle. Step 3: 3/8 turn, obtuse (more than a quarter, less than a half). Step 4: 4/8 = 1/2 turn, a straight angle. (b) 8 steps, since 8 x 1/8 = 1 full turn.
s: Part (a): acute, right, obtuse, straight
Part (b): 8 steps

questions.q: Imran folds a straight angle but the arms do not quite meet: one part comes out a little smaller than the other. Name the kinds of the two angles he gets and say whether either is a right angle.
questions.a: The smaller part is an acute angle and the other is an obtuse angle. Neither is a right angle, because a right angle must be exactly half of a straight angle.
s: Smaller part acute, larger part obtuse
Neither is a right angle, since the halves are unequal

questions.q: Rahul says, 'Whenever a ray OC splits a straight angle AOB, both parts are right angles.' Is he correct? Give the condition under which his claim is true.
questions.a: No. A ray OC can split a straight angle into many pairs of parts, such as one acute and one obtuse. Both parts are right angles only when the two parts are equal, which happens when OC is the crease that makes OB fall on OA.
s: Verdict No
Gives the unequal case (acute and obtuse)
States the condition: the two parts are equal

questions.q: Show that a straight angle cannot be split into two acute angles.
questions.a: A straight angle is two right angles. Each acute angle is less than a right angle, so two acute angles together are less than two right angles. Their sum is therefore less than the straight angle and cannot fill it.
s: A straight angle equals two right angles
Each acute angle is less than a right angle
Their sum is less than a straight angle, so impossible

questions.q: Asha has a slanting crease on a sheet. She marks a point O on it and folds the sheet through O, but the two parts of the slanting crease do not fall on each other. She opens it and finds that the new crease does not look perpendicular. (a) Why does the new crease fail to make right angles? (b) What must be true of the fold for it to work? (c) Why do the angles on the two sides then become right angles?
questions.a: (a) Because the parts of the slanting crease did not coincide, the two angles on either side of the new crease are not equal: one is acute and the other obtuse. (b) The fold must go through O and make the part of the slanting crease on one side fall exactly on the part on the other side. (c) The slanting crease is a straight angle at O, and the fold splits it into two equal angles lying on each other, each half of a straight angle, so each is a right angle.
s: Part (a): the two angles are unequal, one acute and one obtuse
Part (b): the crease must fall on itself through O
Part (c): two equal halves of a straight angle are right angles

questions.q: A straight edge AOB has a point O in the middle. A crease OC is made so that ∠AOC and ∠COB are equal. Then the paper is folded so that OC falls on OA and the crease OD is pressed between OA and OC. (a) What kind of angle is ∠AOC, and what fraction of a full turn is it? (b) What fraction of a full turn is ∠AOD and what kind of angle is it? (c) What fraction of a full turn is ∠DOB and what kind is it? (d) How many times as large as ∠AOD is ∠DOB? (e) Check that ∠AOD and ∠DOB make up a straight angle.
questions.a: (a) A right angle, 1/4 of a full turn. (b) 1/8 of a full turn, an acute angle. (c) 1/8 + 1/4 = 3/8 of a full turn, an obtuse angle. (d) 3 times. (e) 1/8 + 3/8 = 4/8 = 1/2, a half turn, which is a straight angle.
s: Part (a): right angle, 1/4 turn
Part (b): 1/8 turn, acute
Part (c): 3/8 turn, obtuse
Part (d): 3 times

questions.q: A pointer on a dial stops after turning through each of these fractions of a full turn: 1/10, 1/4, 1/3, 3/8, 5/12. (a) Write each turn in degrees. (b) Name the kind of angle each makes. (c) Arrange them from smallest to largest and confirm that every obtuse angle in the list is larger than every acute one. (d) Tina says that 5/12 is 'nearly a half turn, so it is a straight angle'. By how many degrees does it fall short of a straight angle? (e) Another pointer turns 1/4 of a full turn and then 1/10 more in the same direction. What kind of angle has it made?
questions.a: (a) 36°, 90°, 120°, 135°, 150°. (b) Acute, right, obtuse, obtuse, obtuse. (c) 36 < 90 < 120 < 135 < 150; the only acute angle, 36°, is below 90° and all the obtuse ones are above it. (d) 180 - 150 = 30°, so 5/12 falls short by 30° and is not a straight angle. (e) 90° + 36° = 126°, an obtuse angle.
s: Part (b): acute, right, obtuse, obtuse, obtuse
Part (c): ordered list and the acute below the obtuse
Part (d): 30 degrees short, not straight
Part (e): 126 degrees, obtuse

questions.q:
Rohit makes a paper fan in a half circle. He folds a straight edge to make a right angle at O, folds the right angle in half, and then in half again, so the wedges he can cut are 1/4, 1/8 or 1/16 of a full turn. To fill the half circle (a straight angle) with equal wedges, every wedge needs one cut that costs Rs 6, and he has Rs 30. The customer insists that no wedge is wider than 50 degrees.
(a) Give the size of one wedge after each of the three folds as a fraction of a full turn and in degrees, and its kind of angle.
(b) How many equal wedges fill the half circle after each fold?
(c) Find the cut cost for each of the three fan designs.
(d) Which designs meet the customer's condition and the budget? Recommend one and justify.
questions.a: (a) 1/4 = 90° (right angle), 1/8 = 45° (acute) and 1/16 = 22.5° (acute). (b) 2, 4 and 8 wedges (2 x 1/4 = 4 x 1/8 = 8 x 1/16 = 1/2). (c) Rs 12, Rs 24 and Rs 48. (d) The 2-wedge fan has wedges of 90°, wider than 50°. The 8-wedge fan has 22.5° wedges, but costs Rs 48, over Rs 30. Only the 4-wedge fan has 45° wedges, at most 50°, and costs Rs 24, within Rs 30. Recommend the 4-wedge fan.
s: Part (a): 1/4 = 90 right, 1/8 = 45 and 1/16 = 22.5, both acute
Part (b): 2, 4 and 8 wedges
Part (c): Rs 12, 24 and 48
Part (d): rejects 2 wedges (90 degrees too wide) and 8 wedges (Rs 48 over Rs 30), chooses 4 at Rs 24

questions.q: On a wall clock the angle between two successive numbers is the same all round. The hour hand at 12 o'clock points to 12. Through how many degrees has it turned by 8 o'clock?
questions.a: 240°, because each hour is 360° ÷ 12 = 30° and 8 × 30 = 240
o: 240°, because each hour is 360° ÷ 12 = 30° and 8 × 30 = 240
120°, because the hand is 4 hours from 12 the shorter way and 4 × 30 = 120
210°, because 8 hours is 7 whole hours and 7 × 30 = 210

questions.q: A protractor is placed with its centre on the vertex of an angle and one arm along the 0 mark at the right end of the outer scale. The other arm passes through 65 on the outer scale and 115 on the inner scale. What is the measure of the angle?
questions.a: 65°, because the reading must start from the 0 that lies on the arm
o: 65°, because the reading must start from the 0 that lies on the arm
115°, because the larger reading is always the angle
25°, because 90° - 65° is the part left over
180°, because the base line of a protractor is a straight angle

questions.q: The arms OT and OS of an angle pass through the marks 27 and 94 on the same scale of a protractor, with the centre at the vertex O but neither arm on the 0 mark. What is the measure of ∠TOS?
questions.a: 67°, found by subtracting the two readings on the same scale
o: 67°, found by subtracting the two readings on the same scale
121°, found by adding the two readings
94°, because the larger reading is the angle
27°, because the smaller reading is the angle

questions.q: The numbers on a wall clock are equally spaced round the full turn. The hour hand points exactly at 2 and the minute hand exactly at 9. What is the smaller angle between the hands?
Rima makes a paper protractor by folding a semicircle (180°) in half to get 90°, and then folds the 90° and the other 90° each in half once more. Which new crease lies between 90° and 180°?
questions.a: 135°, since the new crease is 45° from the 180° edge
o: 135°, since the new crease is 45° from the 180° edge
120°, since it is a third of the way from 90° to 180°
150°, since it is the middle of the way from 90° to 180°
112.5°, since it is half of the way from 90° to 135°

questions.q: A wheel has 18 equal spokes. The angle between two neighbouring spokes is ___ degrees.

Read these statements about measuring angles.
Statement 1: In a half-circle protractor, each 1° unit is one-hundred-and-eightieth of a straight angle.
Statement 2: An angle of 120° on a half-circle protractor uses 120 of its 180 equal divisions, which is two-thirds of a straight angle.
Statement 3: If an arm passes through the 40 mark on one scale of a protractor, it passes through the 40 mark on the other scale too.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only
all three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The angle between two neighbouring numbers on a clock face is 30°.
Reason (R): A right angle measures 90°.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
The circle is divided into equal parts. Match each fraction of a full turn in Column I with its measure in Column II.
Column I: 1. one-eighth of a full turn  2. one-twelfth of a full turn  3. one-fifth of a full turn  4. one-ninth of a full turn
Column II: A. 30°  B. 45°  C. 40°  D. 72°
The arms OT and OS pass through the marks 35 and 118 on the outer scale of a protractor whose centre is at O. (a) Find ∠TOS. (b) What must you check about the two readings before you subtract?
questions.a: (a) 118° - 35° = 83°. (b) Both readings must be taken on the same scale, because the two scales run in opposite directions.
s: Part (a): 83°
Part (b): both readings from the same scale

questions.q: True or False: An arm that passes through 150 on the outer scale of a semicircular protractor passes through 30 on its inner scale. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The two scales run in opposite directions and each reading and its partner on the other scale add up to 180, as 150 + 30 = 180.
s: Verdict True
Reason: the two readings add up to the straight angle of 180

questions.q: The minute hand of a wall clock, whose numbers are all the same angle apart, moves clockwise from the number 2 to the number 9. (a) Through what angle has it turned, and what kind of angle is that? (b) Yuvraj says the angle is 150°. Name the other turn between the same two positions that is 150°, and show that the two angles together make a full turn.
questions.a: (a) 7 numbers apart, each 30°: 7 x 30° = 210°, a reflex angle. (b) The turn from 9 on to 2 clockwise, passing 12, covers 5 numbers: 5 x 30° = 150°. And 210° + 150° = 360°, a full turn.
s: Part (a): 210 degrees, reflex
Part (b): 150 degrees from 9 to 2 and 210 + 150 = 360

questions.q: A baker cuts a round cake into one piece of 120° for a family order and shares the rest equally into slices of 30° each. (a) How many slices of 30° does he get? (b) What kind of angle is the family's piece, and what is the angle of the whole cake that remains?
questions.a: (a) The rest of the cake is 360° - 120° = 240°, and 240° ÷ 30° = 8 slices. (b) 120° is more than 90° and less than 180°, so the family's piece is an obtuse angle; the cake that remains makes the reflex angle 240°.
s: Part (a): 240 degrees left, 8 slices
Part (b): obtuse, and 240 degrees remains

questions.q: On a semicircular protractor one arm passes through 30 on the outer scale and the other arm passes through 50 on the inner scale, the outer scale starting at 0 on one arm's side. Maya subtracts and writes 50 - 30 = 20°. What mistake has she made and what is the angle?
questions.a: She subtracted readings from two different scales. The other arm reads 180 - 50 = 130 on the outer scale, so the angle is 130 - 30 = 100°.
s: Names the mistake: readings taken from different scales
Converts 50 inner to 130 outer and gets 100°

questions.q: Meera says, 'Whenever an angle in this chapter is bisected, the two halves have a whole number of degrees.' Test her claim with the angles in the paper protractor.
questions.a: No. Bisecting 90° gives 45°, a whole number, but bisecting 45° gives 22.5°, which is not a whole number. The paper protractor itself has creases at 22.5°, 67.5° and so on. So the claim fails once an odd number of degrees is halved.
s: Whole-number case: 90° into 45°
Counter-example: 45° into 22.5°
Verdict No

questions.q: Show that a circle cannot be divided into 7 equal parts each measuring a whole number of degrees.
questions.a: Seven equal parts of a full turn would each have 360° ÷ 7 degrees. But 7 × 51 = 357 and 7 × 52 = 364, so no whole number multiplied by 7 gives 360. Hence the parts cannot have whole-degree measures.
s: Sets the part as 360° ÷ 7
Brackets 360 between 357 and 364
Concludes no whole-number size exists

questions.q: A cupboard door has been opened wider than a straight angle. The protractor shows the smaller angle between the door and the frame as 128°. Zoya writes that the door is opened through 128°, and Nilay writes 232°. (a) Who is right? (b) What kind of angle is the door's opening? (c) What did Zoya read, and what should she have done?
questions.a: (a) Nilay: 360° - 128° = 232°. (b) 232° is greater than 180° and less than 360°, so it is a reflex angle. (c) Zoya read the unmarked (smaller) angle on the protractor, 128°. Because the opening is bigger than a straight angle, she should have subtracted that reading from 360°.
s: Nilay is right: 360 - 128 = 232
Reflex angle with the limits 180 and 360
Zoya gave the unmarked angle instead of subtracting from 360

questions.q: Rima makes a paper protractor from a circle, cutting it into a semicircle (180°) and folding that in half to get 90°. Joy says the next fold will give creases at 60° and 120°, because 180° split into three equal parts gives 60°. (a) Where do the creases from folding each 90° part in half lie, besides 0°, 90° and 180°? (b) Explain Joy's mistake. (c) One more fold makes new creases at 22.5° and 67.5° between 0° and 90°. Find the two new creases between 90° and 180°. (d) What kind of angle does the crease at 112.5° make with the 0° edge, and what kind does the crease at 22.5° make? (e) Show that the crease at 157.5° is as far from the 180° edge as the crease at 22.5° is from the 0° edge.
questions.a: (a) 45° and 135°. (b) Each fold halves a part, so the creases are at half of 90° (45°) and 90° + 45° (135°); making 60° would need folding into three equal parts. (c) 112.5° and 157.5°. (d) 112.5° is more than 90° and less than 180°, so it is obtuse; 22.5° is acute. (e) 180° - 157.5° = 22.5°, the same as 22.5° - 0°.
s: Part (a): 45° and 135°
Part (b): folds halve, they do not divide into three
Part (d): obtuse and acute

questions.q: A semicircular protractor has one scale that starts at 0 on the right end and another that starts at 0 on the left end. The base arm OU lies along the 0 on the right-end scale. The arm OT passes through 20 and the arm OS through 70 on the right-end scale. The arm OR passes through 125 and the arm OQ through 40 on the left-end scale. (a) Find ∠TOS. (b) Find ∠ROT. (c) Find ∠QOS and ∠QOT and name their kinds. (d) The unmarked angle between a sixth arm OP and the arm OT is 105°, and the angle between them is bigger than a straight angle. Find that angle. (e) Dev says ∠ROT = 125° - 20° = 105°. Show that this cannot be right, using the position of OR between OT and OS.
questions.a: (a) 70 - 20 = 50°. (b) OR on the right-end scale reads 180 - 125 = 55, so ∠ROT = 55 - 20 = 35°. (c) OQ reads 180 - 40 = 140 on the right-end scale; ∠QOS = 140 - 70 = 70° (acute) and ∠QOT = 140 - 20 = 120° (obtuse). (d) 360° - 105° = 255°, a reflex angle. (e) OR lies between OT (20) and OS (70), so ∠ROT must be less than ∠TOS = 50°; 105° is more than 50°. Dev used 125, which is a reading on the other scale.
s: Part (a): 50 degrees
Part (b): converts 125 to 55 and gets 35 degrees
Part (c): 70 acute and 120 obtuse
Part (d): 255 degrees
Part (e): OR lies between, so the angle is less than 50; 125 is from the other scale

questions.q:
A school buys 30 protractors with Rs 1,000. The semicircular protractor (a half circle divided into 180 equal parts) costs Rs 25 and the circular one (the full circle divided into 360 equal parts) costs Rs 40. To measure an angle bigger than a straight angle on the semicircular one, a student measures the unmarked angle and subtracts it from 360°, and this extra step takes 1 minute. A worksheet has 20 angles, of which 4 are larger than a straight angle.
(a) Find the cost of 30 protractors of each kind.
(b) For one of the four large angles the unmarked part reads 100°. What is the angle?
(c) What share of the worksheet needs this extra step?
(d) The head compares an all-semicircular purchase with buying 16 circular and 14 semicircular protractors. Find the cost of the second purchase and the minutes lost by all 30 students to the extra step on this worksheet in each case, and recommend one.
questions.a: (a) Semicircular: 30 x 25 = Rs 750; circular: 30 x 40 = Rs 1,200, over the budget. (b) 360° - 100° = 260°. (c) 4 out of 20, that is 20%. (d) The mixed purchase costs 16 x 40 + 14 x 25 = Rs 990, within Rs 1,000. All-semicircular loses 30 x 4 = 120 minutes; in the mixed purchase only the 14 semicircular users lose 14 x 4 = 56 minutes. So Rs 240 more buys 64 minutes. Either choice is accepted if the Rs 240 against 64 minutes is weighed.
s: Part (a): Rs 750 and Rs 1,200
Part (b): 260°
Part (c): 20%
Part (d): Rs 990, 120 against 56 minutes, and a weighed recommendation

questions.q:
A craftsman makes a decorative wheel with equal spokes. The angle between neighbouring spokes must be a whole number of degrees so that it can be marked with a protractor, at most 16° and at least 12° (so that the spokes do not crowd). Each spoke costs Rs 12 and he has Rs 400. He is choosing among 23, 24, 30 and 36 spokes.
(a) Find the angle between neighbouring spokes for 24 and for 30 spokes.
(b) Find the angle for 23 spokes, correct to one decimal place, and for 36 spokes, and say which need each fails.
(c) Find the cost of each wheel.
(d) Which wheels meet every need? Choose one and give your reason.
questions.a: (a) 360° ÷ 24 = 15° and 360° ÷ 30 = 12°. (b) 360° ÷ 23 is about 15.7°, not a whole number, so 23 spokes fail the whole-number need; 360° ÷ 36 = 10°, below 12°, so 36 spokes fail the crowding need. (c) 23 spokes Rs 276, 24 spokes Rs 288, 30 spokes Rs 360, 36 spokes Rs 432 (over Rs 400). (d) 24 spokes (15°, Rs 288) and 30 spokes (12°, Rs 360) both meet every need. Either is accepted with a reason: 24 costs Rs 72 less, while 30 gives a wheel with more spokes at 12°, the narrowest gap allowed.
s: Part (a): 15 and 12 degrees
Part (b): 23 not whole (about 15.7), 36 gives 10 and crowds
Part (d): 24 or 30 spokes, with reason

questions.q: Sana wants to draw ∠XYZ = 40°. She draws the base ray YZ pointing to the left, places the centre of a protractor on Y and lines YZ up with the 0 at the left end of the protractor. Where should she mark X?
questions.a: At 40 on the scale whose 0 lies on the ray YZ, because that scale counts from the base ray
o: At 40 on the scale whose 0 lies on the ray YZ, because that scale counts from the base ray
At 40 on the scale that starts at the right end, because 40 reads the same on both scales
At 140 on the scale whose 0 lies on the ray YZ, because the angle is measured the long way round
At 90, and then rotate the protractor until the arm reaches 40

questions.q: Exactly one of the following pairs contains two angles of different kinds. Which pair is it?
Posts S, G and H stand on a straight fence with G between S and H. A rope GP makes ∠SGP = 65°. Which description of ∠PGH is correct?
questions.a: 115°, an obtuse angle, because ∠SGH is a straight angle of 180°
o: 115°, an obtuse angle, because ∠SGH is a straight angle of 180°
25°, an acute angle, because 90° - 65° = 25°, as for a right angle
65°, an acute angle, because GS and GH are both on the same fence
295°, a reflex angle, because the rope GP lies on the other side

questions.q: Arun has only a semicircular protractor and must draw an angle of 300° at a point O. Which plan gives it?
questions.a: Draw a 60° angle and take the larger region on the other side, as 360° - 60° = 300°
o: Draw a 60° angle and take the larger region on the other side, as 360° - 60° = 300°
Mark 300 on the outer scale, counting on past 180 because the scale continues round
Draw a 150° angle twice, side by side, because 150° + 150° makes the 300° needed
Draw a 120° angle and take the larger region on the other side, since 120° is half of 240°

questions.q: A wheel has 24 equal spokes. Which pair of spokes forms a right angle with the centre?
questions.a: Spokes 6 gaps apart, as 6 × 15° = 90°
o: Spokes 6 gaps apart, as 6 × 15° = 90°
Spokes 4 gaps apart, as 4 × 15° = 60°
Spokes 8 gaps apart, as 8 × 15° = 120°
Spokes 12 gaps apart, as 12 × 15° = 180°

questions.q: A dial has 40 equal divisions round the full turn. The angle at the centre between two marks that are 7 divisions apart is ___ degrees.

Read these statements about classifying angles by degree measure.
Statement 1: An angle of 180° is a reflex angle.
Statement 2: An angle of exactly 90° is an acute angle because it is not more than 90°.
Statement 3: An angle of 181° is a reflex angle.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An angle of 250° is an obtuse angle because it is greater than a right angle.
Reason (R): Reflex angles measure more than 180° and less than 360°.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: Teena wants to draw a 75° angle. She puts the protractor's centre on the vertex and the base ray along the 0 at the left end, but marks the point at 75 on the scale that starts at 0 on the right end. (a) What angle has she actually drawn? (b) Is it the same kind of angle as the one she wanted?
questions.a: (a) That mark is 75 from the right end, so it is 180 - 75 = 105 from the base ray: she drew 105°. (b) No: 75° is acute but 105° is obtuse.
s: Part (a): 105°
Part (b): different kind, acute wanted and obtuse drawn

questions.q: True or False: An angle of 180° and an angle of 181° are the same kind of angle. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. An angle of exactly 180° is a straight angle, and an angle of 181° is more than 180° and less than 360°, so it is a reflex angle.
s: Verdict False
Reason: 180° is straight, 181° is reflex

questions.q: A wheel has 30 equal spokes. (a) Find the angle between two neighbouring spokes. (b) Using (a), find the largest acute angle formed between two spokes.
questions.a: (a) 360° ÷ 30 = 12°. (b) Spokes k gaps apart make 12k°, which is less than 90° only for k = 7, so the largest acute angle is 84° (8 gaps would give 96°, an obtuse angle).
s: Part (a): 12°
Part (b): 84°, with 96° as the next, obtuse value

questions.q: In the guessing game a team scores the difference in degrees between its guess and the true measure. Team 3 guessed 170° for an angle that measured 185°, and 40° for an angle that measured 58°. (a) Find its points. (b) For which guess is the kind of angle wrong, and does the points rule show it?
questions.a: (a) |185 - 170| = 15 and |58 - 40| = 18, so 33 points. (b) The first guess: 170° is obtuse but 185° is a reflex angle. The 15 points are small, so the points rule alone does not show the wrong kind; 40° and 58° are both acute.
s: Part (a): 15 + 18 = 33 points
Part (b): 170 obtuse against 185 reflex, and the points do not show it

questions.q: Imran is told that the unmarked angle between two arms measures 76°, and wants the angle on the other side of the same arms. What is its measure and what kind is it? Why can a protractor not read it directly?
questions.a: The other angle is 360° - 76° = 284°, a reflex angle. A semicircular protractor only goes up to 180°, so the reflex angle has to be found by subtracting the unmarked angle from 360°.
s: 284°, a reflex angle
Reason: the protractor reads only up to 180°, so subtract from 360°

questions.q: Kiran says, 'An angle whose unmarked side reads 137° has a marked side of 233°, and so is a reflex angle.' Is he right?
questions.a: Partly. The kind is right but the measure is wrong. The marked and unmarked angles together make a full turn of 360°, so the marked one is 360° - 137° = 223°, not 233°. Since 223° is more than 180° and less than 360°, it is a reflex angle.
s: Uses the full turn of 360°
Corrects to 223°
Classifies as reflex with the limits 180° and 360°, verdict Partly

questions.q: Show that two acute angles can never add up to a reflex angle.
questions.a: Each acute angle is less than 90°, so the sum of two is less than 90° + 90° = 180°. A reflex angle is more than 180°. So their sum is always smaller than any reflex angle.
s: Each acute angle is less than 90°
The sum is less than 180°
A reflex angle exceeds 180°, so impossible

questions.q: Leela must draw a 65° angle at the point P of a base ray PQ. She puts the protractor's centre on Q, the other end of the ray, with the ray along 0, and marks 65. (a) At which point is the angle she has drawn, and why is it not what she wanted? (b) Where should the centre be placed? (c) Which scale does she read, and what is the other scale's number at that mark?
questions.a: (a) The angle is at Q, because the centre of the protractor sits on the vertex; she wanted the vertex at P. (b) The centre goes on P, with ray PQ along the 0. (c) She reads the scale whose 0 lies on ray PQ, and the other scale reads 180 - 65 = 115 at that mark.
s: Part (a): vertex is at Q, not P
Part (b): centre on P with PQ along 0
Part (c): the scale with 0 on PQ; other scale reads 115

questions.q: The points K, L and M lie on a straight line with L between K and M. Two rays LP and LQ lie on the same side of this line, in the order LK, LP, LQ, LM going round L, with ∠PLK = 58° and ∠QLK = 104°. (a) Find ∠MLP and name its kind. (b) Find ∠QLP and name its kind. (c) Find ∠QLM. (d) Imran says the reflex angle measured the long way round from LK to LP is 302°, and Dev says it is 238°. Who is right, and which angle did the other one find? (e) Check that ∠QLP and ∠QLM add up to ∠MLP.
questions.a: (a) 180° - 58° = 122°, obtuse. (b) 104° - 58° = 46°, acute. (c) 180° - 104° = 76°, acute. (d) 360° - 58° = 302°, so Imran is right; Dev's 238° is 360° - 122°, the reflex angle that goes with ∠MLP, a different angle. (e) 46° + 76° = 122°, which equals ∠MLP.
s: Part (a): 122°, obtuse
Part (b): 46°, acute
Part (c): 76°
Part (d): 302 degrees, and Dev's 238 is the reflex of the angle MLP

questions.q: I am a whole-number acute angle. If you double me, you get an acute angle; triple me, an acute angle again; but if you multiply me by 4 you get an obtuse angle. (a) For each of x = 20, 22, 23, 29, 30 and 31 degrees, find 3 times x and 4 times x and name the kind of each. (b) Which of these six values fit all the clues? (c) Using (a), say which whole numbers from 22 to 30 are possible, and why 22 and 30 are the two boundaries. (d) Check the largest possible value against all three clues. (e) Say what kind of angle 3x is when x = 30, and what kind 4x is when x = 22.
questions.a: (a) 20: 60 acute, 80 acute; 22: 66 acute, 88 acute; 23: 69 acute, 92 obtuse; 29: 87 acute, 116 obtuse; 30: 90 right, 120 obtuse; 31: 93 obtuse, 124 obtuse. (b) 23 and 29 fit (3x acute and 4x obtuse); 20, 22, 30 and 31 do not. (c) 3x must stay below 90, which stops at 29 (30 gives 90, a right angle); 4x must pass 90, which starts at 23 (22 gives 88). So 23 to 29 are possible. (d) 29°: 58° acute, 87° acute, 116° obtuse. (e) 3 x 30 = 90, a right angle, not acute; 4 x 22 = 88, an acute angle, not obtuse.
s: Part (a): the six pairs of values and kinds
Part (b): 23 and 29 fit
Part (c): 23 to 29, boundaries 22 and 30
Part (d): 29 gives 58, 87, 116
Part (e): 90 is right, 88 is acute

questions.q:
A teacher prepares a chart of 10 angles to draw in a 25-minute lesson: 25°, 90°, 140°, 180°, 230°, 75°, 310°, 60°, 200° and 115°. With her semicircular protractor each angle up to 180° takes 2 minutes to draw, and each reflex angle takes 4 minutes because she must work from the unmarked angle. A circular protractor can be hired for Rs 30 for the day and takes 2 minutes for every angle.
(a) How many of the 10 angles are acute, how many obtuse, how many reflex, and how many are none of these three?
(b) How long does the whole chart take with the semicircular protractor?
(c) How long with the hired circular protractor?
(d) Advise the teacher, using the lesson time and the hire cost.
questions.a: (a) Acute: 25°, 75°, 60° (3). Obtuse: 140°, 115° (2). Reflex: 230°, 310°, 200° (3). Neither: 90° (right) and 180° (straight), so 2; 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10. (b) 7 x 2 + 3 x 4 = 26 minutes. (c) 10 x 2 = 20 minutes. (d) The semicircular one takes 26 minutes, 1 minute over the lesson. She can either pay Rs 30 to finish in 20 minutes with 5 spare, or drop one angle from the chart and stay within 25 minutes at no cost. Any reasoned choice is accepted.
s: Part (a): 3 acute, 2 obtuse, 3 reflex
Part (b): 26 minutes
Part (c): 20 minutes
Part (d): compares the 1-minute overrun with Rs 30 and recommends

questions.q:
In a guessing game each team scores the difference in degrees between its guess and the true measure of an angle, and the lowest total over five rounds wins. Team 2 guessed 39°, 90°, 110°, 70° and 30° for angles measuring 49°, 83°, 120°, 65° and 17°. Team 1 guessed 28°, 96°, 80°, 130° and 65° for angles measuring 34°, 105°, 72°, 150° and 58°.
(a) Find each team's total score and the winner.
(b) In how many rounds did each team guess an angle of a different kind (acute, right or obtuse) from the true angle?
(c) The class proposes adding a penalty of 10 points for every guess of the wrong kind. Find the new totals.
(d) Should the class adopt the penalty? Give your judgement.
questions.a: (a) Team 2: 10 + 7 + 10 + 5 + 13 = 45; Team 1: 6 + 9 + 8 + 20 + 7 = 50. Team 2 wins. (b) Team 2 once (a guess of 90°, a right angle, for an acute 83°); Team 1 never. (c) Team 2: 45 + 10 = 55; Team 1: 50, so Team 1 wins. (d) With the penalty the winner changes, so it matters. A penalty rewards knowing the kind of angle, which is the skill the chapter teaches, but it adds 10 points to a guess that was only 7 degrees out, so a guess of 90° for 83° (17 points) is punished almost as hard as an 18-degree error of the right kind (18 points). Either decision is accepted if it is argued from these totals.
s: Part (a): 45 and 50, Team 2 wins
Part (b): Team 2 once, Team 1 none
Part (c): 55 and 50
Part (d): a judgement using that the winner changes
